rv.q: The house might have been built for him, but Alexander McQueen is not at home.
Unfortunately, despite the first-class production, House of McQueen never quite comes to dramatic life.
These efforts pay off in visual splendor. Yet, in part because of the great inherent promise of its subject, “House of McQueen” feels mostly like a missed opportunity.

No doubt the show’s makers intend to celebrate McQueen’s ideals and achievements in the face of awesome challenges. Rather than mount an overstuffed hagiography, surely a daring, provocative artist like McQueen deserves some sort of outrageous theater treatment. Perhaps McQueen’s life might be bette...
House of McQueen is mostly a house of cards.
If it weren’t based on a true story, it would be gratuitous. Even as it stands, the play teeters on overwhelming its audience with trauma.

Darrah Cloud’s fever dream of a script, which is made up short scenes that jump around in time and place, is a crazy quilt of incomprehensibility that seems to lift its limited plot points from Wikipedia.

To Cloud’s credit though, the emotional, gut-wrenching moments in the play will certainly hit the audience like a shot in the heart (and will leave them in tears). Overall, “House of McQueen” is a bold, daring, flamboyant, yet entertaining new play that pays homage to the late but great Alexander McQueen.
